newsitem.title: UK: Labour's Blair goes on offensive over health.
newsitem.headline: Labour's Blair goes on offensive over health.

text.p: Labour leader Tony Blair on Thursday sailed above the rows over Europe tearing apart the ruling Conservatives to hammer home his message of the day that only Labour could be trusted to protect the health service.

Aides said Blair was delighted that the Conservatives' civil war on Europe was once more exposing Prime Minister John Major's weak leadership but wanted to stick to issues that were of more pressing concern to most voters.
At a rally in the Scottish capital, Blair warned that a vote to re-elect the Conservatives on May 1 for a fifth consecutive time would give them a licence to kill the National Health Service (NHS).
"For make no mistake: they are killing the National Health Service as we know it," Blair said in prepared remarks.

He said waiting lists for operations were rising, one in four hospital beds had closed since 1989 and the cost of administering the service had jumped since then by 1.5 billion pounds because of a 20,000 increase in the number of managers.
Blair believes health is an area in which he can demonstrate Labour would make a big difference, despite tight financial constraints.

Labour plans to channel 100 million pounds ($160 million) saved by cutting red tape into front-line patient care. It would also replace the internal market introduced by the Conservatives with a system whereby local doctors cooperate instead of compete to purchase care for the whole community.
Although Major has said he would never privatise the NHS "while I live and breathe", Blair said that, if re-elected, the Conservatives would gradually give the private sector a bigger role.
"Stop saying the NHS is safe in your hands when your reforms are slowly strangling it to death," he said.
Among the entertainers due to warm up the crowd for Blair were the pop group D:Ream, whose hit "Things Can Only Get Better" has been adopted by Labour as their campaign anthem.
Before the rally, Blair passed up a chance to answer questions on Europe as he was photographed in an Edinburgh hotel pulling glasses of "Blair's Brew", a specially produced Scottish ale.
Not even the reappearance of a kilted actor wearing a chicken outfit, sent by the Conservatives to taunt Blair for his refusal to debate Major on television, could disturb the Labour leader's calm.
Sitting on a runaway poll lead with just two weeks to election day, he knows he can choose the ground on which he wants to fight. ($1=.6141 Pound)
